Skip to content
SOTS explainer / local draft
SOTS DOTS SQUISH DP Compare Correctness References

Local draft · grounded in this repository

Simplification of Trajectory Streams

How the current streaming \(\delta\)-simplification algorithm works, and how this project actually runs DOTS, SQUISH, and Douglas-Peucker as baselines - with the math the sources support, and no stronger claims.

Sources: Cheng, Huang, Jiang, Simplification of Trajectory Streams (arXiv:2503.23025, papers/journal.pdf); simplify.cpp / simplify_geometry.h; vendored baselines under traj-compression/. Design tokens follow the web visualizer in web/index.html.

What this page will not do

It does not invent Fréchet bounds for DOTS, SQUISH, or DP. Those tools in this repo optimize (or heuristically reduce) different errors. The \((1+\varepsilon)\delta\) Fréchet guarantee below is the paper's claim for Algorithm 1, which this binary implements in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Implementation shortcuts versus the paper are labeled as such.

The problem

A GPS-style sensor emits vertices \(v_1, v_2, \ldots\) in order. The prefix so far is the polygonal curve \(\tau[v_1,v_i]\). A simplifier should emit a much shorter curve \(\sigma\) without keeping the whole history in working storage, and without waiting for the stream to end.

This project's paper measures similarity with the continuous Fréchet distance. Parameterizations \(\rho_\sigma, \rho_\tau : [0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^d\) move from start to end without backtracking. A matching \(M\) pairs \(\rho_\sigma(t)\) with \(\rho_\tau(t)\). Then

$$d_F(\sigma,\tau)=\inf_M \max_{t\in[0,1]} d\bigl(\rho_\sigma(t),\rho_\tau(t)\bigr).$$

Two problems appear in the paper (journal §1):

  • \(\delta\)-simplification. Given \(\delta>0\), minimize \(|\sigma|\) subject to \(d_F(\sigma,\tau)\le\delta\). Write \(\kappa(\tau,\delta)\) for that minimum size.
  • \(k\)-simplification. Given an integer \(k\ge 2\), minimize \(d_F(\sigma,\tau)\) subject to \(|\sigma|\le k\).

This repository implements \(\delta\)-simplification

The headless binary simplify is Algorithm 1 of the paper (journal §2), in the plane. The \(k\)-simplification procedures Reduce / Compress (journal §3, Algorithms 2-3) are not in simplify.cpp. CLI defaults in simplify_io.h are \(\delta=200\) and \(\varepsilon=0.5\), overridable with -d and -e.

Figure 1. Fréchet is a leash: both walkers move forward, and the leash is the worst-case pairing distance. A single shortcut can still be close in \(d_F\) if it stabs a tube around \(\tau\).

1. Current algorithm: streaming \(\delta\)-simplification

Intuition from journal §1.2: find a line segment that stabs as many consecutive vertex-balls of radius \((1+O(\varepsilon))\delta\) as possible. When a new vertex makes that impossible, emit the segment sitting in a one-edge buffer and start a new segment. Concatenating those segments is \(\sigma\).

Inputs, parameters, and output

Input stream

data/<id>/original.txt: first line \(N\), then \(N\) lines of \(x\ y\) (no timestamps). Parsed in read_stream (simplify_io.h).

Parameters

\(\delta\) (-d, corridor / error budget) and \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) (-e, approximation slack). Web UI labels these Match / Grid; the math is still \(\varepsilon,\delta\).

Online order

simplify() walks \(cur=0,1,\ldots\) and repeatedly calls get_longest_stab. Each call consumes a maximal prefix and appends two points (segment endpoints) to the output.

What is emitted

Vertices of \(\sigma\) are grid / hull points, not necessarily vertices of \(\tau\). The paper explicitly allows this. Optional --dist measures continuous Fréchet via scripts/frechet.jl (FrechetDist.jl).

Grid cover of the \(\delta\)-disk

Fix a vertex \(x\). Let \(B_x\) be the ball of radius \(\delta\) at \(x\). Journal §2 uses an axis-aligned grid with \(x\) as a grid vertex and side length

$$\frac{\varepsilon\delta}{2\sqrt{d}}.$$

In this codebase \(d=2\), so GRID_val is \(\varepsilon\delta/(2\sqrt{2})\). Let \(G_x\) be the grid cells that meet the slightly larger ball of radius \((1+\varepsilon/2)\delta\) (R_val). Then \(\mathrm{conv}(G_x)\) is a convex inner/outer stand-in for that disk. An oriented segment \(s\) stabs objects \(O_1,\ldots,O_m\) in order if there are points \(x_i\in s\cap O_i\) appearing in that order along \(s\).

Figure 2. Covering the vertex disk by a coarse grid. Farthest grid-corner offset is stored as expected_frechet_squared; its square root is the implementation's a-priori leash length (at most about \((1+\varepsilon)\delta\) when the formulas match the paper).

Reachable stab regions and the free-space wedge

After choosing a start vertex \(v_i\), let \(P\) be a discrete set of candidate start points on the grid of \(G_{v_i}\). The paper takes all grid points of \(G_{v_i}\) (\(|P|=O(\varepsilon^{-d})\)). For each \(p\in P\):

$$S_i[p]=\{p\},\qquad S_{a+1}[p]=\mathrm{conv}(G_{v_{a+1}})\cap F\bigl(S_a[p],p\bigr),$$

where the free-space set is

$$F(S,p)=\{\,y\in\mathbb{R}^d : py\cap S\neq\emptyset\,\}.$$

If \(p\in S\), then \(F(S,p)=\mathbb{R}^d\). If \(S=\emptyset\), then \(F=\emptyset\). Otherwise \(F\) is the unbounded convex “shadow” of \(S\) seen from light source \(p\) (journal §2.1). find_F builds that wedge clipped to the working bounding box; intersect clips it against \(\mathrm{conv}(G_i)\) with Sutherland-Hodgman.

Figure 3. One candidate start \(p\). The next hull must meet the wedge of rays through the current stab region \(S\). Empty intersection: that \(p\) is marked dead in get_longest_stab.

The longest-stab loop (what the code does)

For a prefix starting at stream[cur]:

  1. Build boundary anchors \(P\) around \(p_0\) (get_boundary_points_from_grid).
  2. Initialize each \(S[i]=\{P[i]\}\), all alive.
  3. For each later point \(v\): hull \(G_i=\mathrm{conv}(G_v)\); for each live \(p\), set \(S\leftarrow F(S,p)\cap G_i\). If none survive, stop.
  4. While someone is alive, keep a two-point buffer \((p,q)\) from the highest-index live candidate (\(q\) is new_S[i].front()).
  5. Emit the buffer; return the index of the first unstabbed vertex, which becomes the next \(p_0\).

Paper vs this binary

  • Journal Algorithm 1 uses all grid points of \(G_{v_i}\) as \(P\). This repo uses the discrete outline of that sample set (leftmost/rightmost point of every grid row, plus the full top and bottom rows). Size bounds proved for the full \(P\) should not be assumed to transfer automatically.
  • \(F\) is clipped to a padded axis-aligned bbox (configure_bbox), not \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
  • \(\mathrm{conv}(G_i)\) is a cached origin-centred hull translated by the current vertex (same shape at every point).
  • The paper's \(k\)-simplification path is unused here.

The inner loop, from simplify.cpp:

Figure 4. Each longest-stab emits two points. The blue joints are the paper's extra edges that connect the end of \(s_j\) to the start of \(s_{j+1}\). Those joints are why the size bound is \(2\kappa-2\), not \(\kappa\).

Guarantees stated for Algorithm 1 (journal Lemma 2, Theorem 3)

For every prefix \(\tau[v_1,v_i]\), the paper's \(\sigma\) satisfies

$$d_F\bigl(\sigma,\tau[v_1,v_i]\bigr)\le(1+\varepsilon)\delta,\qquad |\sigma|\le 2\kappa\bigl(\tau[v_1,v_i],\delta\bigr)-2.$$

Working storage \(O(\varepsilon^{-\alpha})\) with \(\alpha=2(d-1)\lfloor d/2\rfloor^2+d\) (Theorem 3). For \(d=2\), \(\alpha=4\). These are claims about Algorithm 1 as written in the paper, not about DOTS/SQUISH/DP, and not automatically about the boundary-\(P\) shortcut in this binary. See Correctness.

2. DOTS

as-you-go DOTS is “Directed acyclic graph based Online Trajectory Simplification” (Cao and Li). It is a vertex-subset online method for the min-\(\#\) problem under a local integral squared SED budget, not under Fréchet.

Error: SED and LSSD / LISSED

Synchronized Euclidean distance compares a dropped point \(p_k=(x_k,y_k,t_k)\) to the linearly interpolated location on the shortcut \(p_i p_j\):

$$x'_k=x_i+\frac{t_k-t_i}{t_j-t_i}(x_j-x_i),\qquad \mathrm{SED}_k=\sqrt{(x_k-x'_k)^2+(y_k-y'_k)^2}.$$

DOTS accumulates squared SEDs between indices \(i\) and \(j\):

$$\mathrm{LISSED}_{ij}=\sum_{i<k<j}\mathrm{SED}_k^2.$$

Prefix sums make each \(\mathrm{LISSED}_{ij}\) \(O(1)\) (DOTS paper §2; DotsSimplifier::getLSSD). In this project, input files have no timestamps, so dots.cpp assigns \(t=0,1,2,\ldots\).

Figure 5. Sketch of DOTS (paper Figs. 2 and 4; directedAcyclicGraphSearch). An edge exists when \(\mathrm{LISSED}_{ij}\) is below the threshold. When every current parent is terminated or \(|V_L|\) hits maxVkSize, DOTS swaps layers, locally minimizes integral SSED, and emits indices that all surviving paths agree on.

How this repo invokes DOTS

  • Source: traj-compression/online/DOTS/ (submodule https://github.com/yeungsinchun/traj-compression.git), built as target dots (CMakeLists.txt).
  • CLI: ./build/dots <id> -lssd <threshold> writes data/<id>/dots_simplified.txt. Default threshold in dots.cpp is \(0.05\); the web compare pane defaults to \(10^6\) (UI shows thousands).
  • Web: GET /api/trace/<id>/compare?algorithm=dots&run=1&lssd=... in web/server.py.
  • Benchmark: scripts/benchmark.py runs DOTS with -lssd 200000, measures Fréchet \(d\) of that output, then runs simplify with \(\varepsilon=d-1\) and \(\delta=1\) (skipping if \(\varepsilon\le 0\)). That pairing is a benchmark protocol, not a theorem.
  • Call used by the binary: DotsSimplifier::batchDotsByIndex (online algorithm invoked on the whole file).

DOTS paper complexity: \(O(N^2/M)\) per their analysis, with a cascaded \(O(N)\) variant. This project's wrapper uses the non-cascade batchDotsByIndex path. No Fréchet bound is claimed in DotsSimplifier.h.

3. SQUISH

keep % SQUISH (Spatial QUalIty Simplification Heuristic; Muckell et al.) is an online buffer algorithm. One parameter is the buffer capacity. This repo exposes it as a keep ratio in \((0,1]\): max_buffer_size = ratio * n (at least 2).

Each interior point stores a Synchronized Euclidean Distance versus its current neighbors (again with index-as-time in the adapted binary). When the buffer overflows, the interior point of smallest SED is dropped, and that SED is added to both neighbors (a local heuristic, not a globally recomputed priority queue).

$$ \mathrm{SED}(s,m,e)=\bigl\| m - \bigl(s+\tfrac{t_m-t_s}{t_e-t_s}(e-s)\bigr)\bigr\|_2 $$

Figure 6. Algorithm 1 of the SQUISH paper, as implemented in traj-compression/online/SQUISH/SQUISH_adapted.cpp. Endpoints are never removed. The paper does not prove a Fréchet bound; this repo does not add one.

How this repo invokes SQUISH

  • Built as squish from SQUISH_adapted.cpp when that file exists.
  • CLI: ./build/squish <input.txt> <ratio> <output.txt> with ratio∈(0,1].
  • Web default keep fraction \(0.2\) (UI: 20%). Compare API: algorithm=squish&ratio=0.2.
  • Not used by scripts/benchmark.py (that script compares only against DOTS).

4. Douglas-Peucker (DP)

all-at-once Classic batch line simplification (Douglas and Peucker, 1973). This repo's adapted binary uses perpendicular Euclidean distance (PED) from each interior point to the chord, not SED and not Fréchet.

On a range \([s,\ell]\), find the farthest interior point \(i^\star\). If that PED is \(\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DP}}\), keep only the endpoints. Otherwise recurse on \([s,i^\star]\) and \([i^\star,\ell]\) and concatenate. Output is a subsequence of the original vertices. The whole curve must be present: this is offline.

Figure 7. PED farthest-point recursion as in douglasPeucker in DP_adapted.cpp. Step through. The gold point is the current farthest vertex from the active chord. Recursion is the reason DP cannot emit a prefix until the full polyline is known.

How this repo invokes DP

  • Built as dp from traj-compression/batch/DP/DP_adapted.cpp.
  • CLI: ./build/dp <input.txt> <epsilon> <output.txt>. Web default PED \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DP}}=0.9\).
  • Compare API: algorithm=dp&epsilon=0.9. Output data/<id>/dp_simplified.txt.
  • Like SQUISH, DP is a web-pane baseline, not part of benchmark.py.

Worst-case time of this naive recursion is \(\Theta(n^2)\); typical cartographic analyses quote \(O(n\log n)\) with hull tricks (the SQUISH paper's Table 1 lists \(O(n\log n)\) for DP). The adapted file does not use hull acceleration.

5. Comparison sketch

These four families are not interchangeable “better/worse” Fréchet compressors. They answer different questions, and this repo wires them as overlay baselines in web/.

Family Mode in this repo Parameter Error notion Vertices of \(\sigma\) When it applies
SOTS Algorithm 1 Streaming prefixes; emit as you go \(\varepsilon,\delta\) Continuous Fréchet; paper: \(d_F\le(1+\varepsilon)\delta\) Grid / hull points (not required to be in \(\tau\)) Need a global leash bound while vertices arrive; can spend poly\((1/\varepsilon)\) working storage independent of \(n\)
DOTS Online DAG (batch wrapper on a file) LSSD threshold Local integral squared SED; near-optimal min-\(\#\) for that budget (authors' claim) Subset of \(\tau\) Need a vertex subsequence with a time-synchronized squared-error budget; timestamps matter (here: indices)
SQUISH Online fixed buffer Keep ratio (buffer size) Heuristic SED; no Fréchet theorem in the paper Subset of \(\tau\) Hard cap on stored points; streaming GPS with a priority-style drop
DP Batch recursion PED \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DP}}\) Hausdorff-style perpendicular distance to chords, not \(d_F\) Subset of \(\tau\) Whole curve is already in memory; cartographic polyline thinning

Streaming vs batch

SOTS, DOTS, and SQUISH can update on each arrival. DP's farthest-point split needs the current range's last vertex, so a true stream cannot finish the first recursive call until EOF. The web UI therefore glosses DP as “all-at-once” and DOTS as “as-you-go”.

Fair numeric comparison?

benchmark.py only equalizes against DOTS, and even then by setting simplify's \(\varepsilon\) from DOTS's measured Fréchet minus one, with \(\delta=1\). That is an experimental matching rule, not an equivalence of error semantics. The VLDB 2018 survey in papers/benchmark.pdf is the broader 25-algorithm quality study this submodule originally supported.

6. Correctness (from the paper, not invented)

Only SOTS has a Fréchet proof in the sources this page is allowed to use. Below is an outline of journal §2.2. Full proofs stay in the PDF / arXiv; this is a map, not a substitute.

Invariant (Lemma 1(i))

Start with \(S_i[p]=p\) for every grid point \(p\in P\subset G_{v_i}\). For \(j>i\) while the regions stay nonempty,

$$S_j[p]=\bigl\{x\in\mathrm{conv}(G_{v_j}): px\text{ stabs }\mathrm{conv}(G_{v_i}),\ldots,\mathrm{conv}(G_{v_j})\text{ in order}\bigr\}.$$

Proof outline. Base \(j=i+1\): \(S_{i+1}[p]=\mathrm{conv}(G_{v_{i+1}})\). Inductive step: \(x\in F(S_{j-1}[p],p)\) iff \(px\) meets \(S_{j-1}[p]\), which by induction means \(px\) already stabs the earlier hulls; intersecting with the next hull adds the last stab. Conversely, a stabbing segment through the next hull already hit \(S_{j-1}[p]\). (Journal p. 6, after Figure 1.)

Quality (Lemma 2)

Error. A emitted segment \(s=pq\) stabs \(\mathrm{conv}(G_{v_a})\) in order, and each hull sits inside the ball of radius \((1+\varepsilon)\delta\) about \(v_a\) (grid corner offset \(\le\varepsilon\delta/2\) on top of radius \((1+\varepsilon/2)\delta\)). Linear interpolation along the stabs is a Fréchet matching of leash \((1+\varepsilon)\delta\). Joints between consecutive emitted segments are matched the same way.

Size. Let \(\gamma=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)\) be an optimal \(\delta\)-simplification, \(k=\kappa(\tau[v_1,v_i],\delta)\). A Fréchet matching of \(\gamma\) to \(\tau\) maps vertices \(v_a\) to points \(x_a\) on \(\gamma\). Charge the first emitted segment to edge \(u_1u_2\): there is a grid point \(p\) within \(\varepsilon\delta/2\) of \(x_1\), and \(pu_2\) still stabs the \((1+\varepsilon/2)\delta\) balls, so Algorithm 1 cannot have been forced to emit earlier. Repeat along \(\gamma\). At most \(k-1\) emitted stabs, plus at most \(k-2\) connecting edges, hence \(|\sigma|\le 2k-2\). (Journal Lemma 2, Figure 2.)

Where the charging needs the full grid \(P\)

The “grid point \(p\) within \(\varepsilon\delta/2\) of \(x_1\)” may lie in the interior of \(G_{v_1}\). Algorithm 1 as proved therefore keeps all grid points. This binary's boundary-only \(P\) is an implementation choice; do not treat Lemma 2's size bound as a theorem about get_boundary_points_from_grid unless a separate argument is written.

Complexity (Theorem 3)

Lemma 2 gives quality. Remaining work: bound the combinatorial complexity of \(S_j[p]\) and \(F(S_{j-1}[p],p)\). Non-pivot facets of \(S_j[p]\) inherit outward normals from the translated hulls \(\mathrm{conv}(G_{v_a})\), so there are \(O(\varepsilon^{(1-d)\lfloor d/2\rfloor})\) of them. Pivot facets (hyperplanes through \(p\) tangent to an earlier region) charge to ordered pairs of those normals without reuse, hence \(O(\varepsilon^{2(1-d)\lfloor d/2\rfloor})\) pivots. With \(|P|=O(\varepsilon^{-d})\) this yields working storage \(O(\varepsilon^{-\alpha})\) for \(\alpha=2(d-1)\lfloor d/2\rfloor^2+d\). Processing time per vertex is \(O(\varepsilon^{-\alpha}\log(1/\varepsilon))\) in dimensions 2 and 3. (Journal Theorem 3, pp. 8-9, Figure 3.)

What is not proved here

  • \(k\)-simplification (Lemmas 4-8, Algorithms 2-3): exists in the paper; not this binary.
  • DOTS: authors argue near-optimality of min-\(\#\) for a LISSED threshold via DAG shortest paths; that is a different theorem, about SED, in papers/dots.pdf.
  • SQUISH: heuristic; the paper reports empirical SED versus Uniform Sampling, DP, and Dead Reckoning. No Fréchet lemma.
  • DP: the PED threshold is an invariant of the recursion (every discarded point has PED \(\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DP}}\) to its surviving chord). That does not imply \(d_F\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{DP}}\).

Key code paths

Sutherland-Hodgman clip of \(F\) against \(\mathrm{conv}(G_i)\), plus the grid helpers:

References

  1. Siu-Wing Cheng, Haoqiang Huang, Le Jiang. Simplification of Trajectory Streams. 2025. arXiv:2503.23025. Local PDF: papers/journal.pdf. Algorithm 1, Lemma 1-2, Theorem 3, §2.
  2. Weiquan Cao, Yunzhao Li. DOTS: An online and near-optimal trajectory simplification algorithm. Geoinformatica manuscript. Local PDF: papers/dots.pdf. Vendored code: traj-compression/online/DOTS/ (DotsSimplifier.h, dots.cpp).
  3. Jonathan Muckell, Vikram Patil, Fan Ping, Jeong-Hyon Hwang, Catherine T. Lawson, S. S. Ravi. SQUISH: An Online Approach for GPS Trajectory Compression. Local PDF: papers/squish.pdf. Algorithm 1. Vendored code: traj-compression/online/SQUISH/SQUISH_adapted.cpp.
  4. David H. Douglas, Thomas K. Peucker. Algorithms for the reduction of the number of points required to represent a digitized line or its caricature. Cartographica, 1973. This repo: traj-compression/batch/DP/DP_adapted.cpp (PED recursion).
  5. Dongxiang Zhang, Mengting Ding, Dingyu Yang, Yi Liu, Ju Fan, Heng Tao Shen. Trajectory Simplification: An Experimental Study and Quality Analysis. PVLDB 11(9):934-946, 2018. DOI 10.14778/3213880.3213885. Local PDF: papers/benchmark.pdf. Origin of the traj-compression collection.
  6. This repository, README and CLI: README.md, simplify.cpp, simplify_geometry.h, simplify_io.h, CMakeLists.txt.
  7. Web compare wiring: web/server.py (/api/trace/<id>/compare), web/viewer.js, web/index.html.
  8. DOTS-only benchmark protocol: scripts/benchmark.py (LSSD \(200000\); then simplify with \(\varepsilon=d_F^{\mathrm{DOTS}}-1\), \(\delta=1\)).
  9. Continuous Fréchet post-check: scripts/frechet.jl, wrapping FrechetDist.jl.
  10. Baseline submodule: yeungsinchun/traj-compression (.gitmodules). The algorithms/ tree mentioned in the README is not present in this checkout.

int get_longest_stab(const std::vector<Point>& stream, int cur,
                     std::vector<Point>& simplified,
                     double EPSILON, double DELTA) {
    const Point& p0 = stream[cur];
    std::vector<Point> P = get_boundary_points_from_grid(p0, EPSILON, DELTA);
    std::array<Point, 2> buffer = {p0, p0};
    // live candidates S[i] start at P[i]; die when F(S,p) misses conv(G_i)
    // buffer keeps (p, q) from the last surviving candidate
    simplified.emplace_back(buffer[0]);
    simplified.emplace_back(buffer[1]);
    return cur;
}

inline double GRID_val(double EPSILON, double DELTA, int multiplier = 1) {
    return EPSILON * DELTA / (2.0 * std::sqrt(2.0)) / multiplier;
}
inline double R_val(double EPSILON, double DELTA) {
    return (1.0 + EPSILON / 2.0) * DELTA;
}
// F(S,p): bbox-clipped wedge of rays from p through convex S
inline void find_F(const Point& p, const std::vector<Point>& S,
                   std::vector<Point>& F);
// Convex-convex clip used as F(S,p) intersect conv(G_i)
inline bool intersect(const std::vector<Point>& P_in,
                      const std::vector<Point>& Q_in,
                      std::vector<Point>& result);

    ];
    const overlay = document.getElementById("dp-overlay");
    const cap = document.getElementById("dp-caption");
    const captions = [
      "Step 0. Chord from first to last. Every interior PED is measured to this one segment.",
      "Step 1. Farthest point exceeds eps_DP, so split there (gold).",
      "Step 2. Left subproblem: farthest on the left chord.",
      "Step 3. Right subproblem: farthest on the right chord. Batch: both sides needed."
    ];
    function line(a, b, color, width) {
      const e = document.createElementNS("http://www.w3.org/2000/svg", "line");
      e.setAttribute("x1", a[0]); e.setAttribute("y1", a[1]);
      e.setAttribute("x2", b[0]); e.setAttribute("y2", b[1]);
      e.setAttribute("stroke", color); e.setAttribute("stroke-width", width);
      return e;
    }
    function dot(pt, color, r) {
      const e = document.createElementNS("http://www.w3.org/2000/svg", "circle");
      e.setAttribute("cx", pt[0]); e.setAttribute("cy", pt[1]);
      e.setAttribute("r", r || 7); e.setAttribute("fill", color);
      return e;
    }
    function ped(a, m, b) {
      const A = b[0]-a[0], B = a[1]-b[1], C = b[1]*a[0]-a[1]*b[0];
      const den = Math.hypot(A, B);
      if (den === 0) return 0;
      return Math.abs(A*m[1] + B*m[0] + C) / den;
    }
    function farthest(i, j) {
      let best = i+1, dmax = -1;
      for (let k = i+1; k < j; k++) {
        const d = ped(dpPts[i], dpPts[k], dpPts[j]);
        if (d > dmax) { dmax = d; best = k; }
      }
      return best;
    }
    function showDp(step) {
      overlay.replaceChildren();
      cap.textContent = captions[step];
      const n = dpPts.length-1;
      if (step === 0) {
        overlay.append(line(dpPts[0], dpPts[n], "#a78bfa", 3));
      } else if (step === 1) {
        const f = farthest(0, n);
        overlay.append(line(dpPts[0], dpPts[n], "#a78bfa", 2));
        overlay.append(dot(dpPts[f], "#fbbf24"));
        overlay.append(line(dpPts[f], [(dpPts[0][0]+dpPts[n][0])/2, (dpPts[0][1]+dpPts[n][1])/2], "#fbbf24", 1.2));
      } else if (step === 2) {
        const f = farthest(0, n);
        overlay.append(line(dpPts[0], dpPts[f], "#a78bfa", 3));
        overlay.append(line(dpPts[f], dpPts[n], "#262b36", 2));
        overlay.append(dot(dpPts[f], "#3ddc97"));
        overlay.append(dot(dpPts[farthest(0, f)], "#fbbf24"));
      } else {
        const f = farthest(0, n);
        overlay.append(line(dpPts[0], dpPts[f], "#262b36", 2));
        overlay.append(line(dpPts[f], dpPts[n], "#a78bfa", 3));
        overlay.append(dot(dpPts[f], "#3ddc97"));
        overlay.append(dot(dpPts[farthest(f, n)], "#fbbf24"));
      }
      document.querySelectorAll("[data-dp]").forEach((b) => {
        b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", b.getAttribute("data-dp") === String(step) ? "true" : "false");
      });
    }
    document.querySelectorAll("[data-dp]").forEach((b) => {
      b.addEventListener("click", () => showDp(Number(b.getAttribute("data-dp"))));
    });
    showDp(0);
  })();

            if (!intersect(F[i], Gi, new_S[i])) {

            buffer[0] = P[i];
            buffer[1] = new_S[i].front();
            has_candidate = true;
        }
        if (!has_candidate || dead_cnt == Pn) break;
        for (int i = 0; i < Pn; ++i)
            if (!dead[i]) S[i].swap(new_S[i]);
        cur++;
    }
    simplified.emplace_back(buffer[0]);
    simplified.emplace_back(buffer[1]);
    return cur;
}
